WSET exam preparation: choose your level and study with a method

Good WSET preparation means three things: picking the level that matches your knowledge, studying the syllabus chapter by chapter with active recall, and rehearsing the real exam format before the day. The Wine Goat is an independent app that turns this into a daily plan, with lessons, practice questions, flashcards and mock exams for Wine Levels 1–3 and Spirits Levels 1–2.

Whether you are a curious drinker, a sommelier in training or someone who sells wine and spirits every day, a WSET qualification rewards steady, well-organised study far more than last-minute cramming. The course gives you the content; how you revise it decides how calm and confident you feel in the exam room.

This page brings together everything you need to start: how the levels differ, how much time each one asks for, a study method that works at every level, the most common mistakes, and how The Wine Goat can support your preparation in English, Italian, French or Spanish.
How do you prepare for a WSET exam?

Prepare in three phases: learn the syllabus chapter by chapter, consolidate it with practice questions and flashcards every day, then rehearse the real exam with timed mock exams in the final weeks. Each phase needs a small, regular effort rather than long weekend sessions.

The WSET qualifications are taught by independent course providers, in a classroom or online, and every level ends with a closed-book exam organised by your provider. Your course gives you the structure and the textbook. What happens between lessons is up to you, and that is where most results are decided: people who review a little every day remember far more than people who reread their notes the night before.

A useful way to think about it is that the course teaches you the material once, while revision makes sure you can retrieve it under time pressure. Reading feels productive, but answering questions, recalling facts from memory and explaining ideas in your own words are what actually build exam-ready knowledge.

A study method that works at every level

The most reliable method combines four habits: learn in small chapters, test yourself straight away, repeat what you forget at increasing intervals, and practise the exact exam format. These habits are backed by decades of research on memory and they suit busy schedules.
1. Learn one chapter at a time

Follow the order of the syllabus and finish one topic before moving on: grape varieties, then a region, then winemaking or distillation. Short lessons of ten to fifteen minutes are easier to fit into a day and easier to remember than a two-hour reading session.
2. Test yourself immediately

After each lesson, answer a set of questions on the same chapter. Retrieving information from memory, even when you get it wrong, strengthens it more than rereading. Always read the explanation, and especially why the other options are wrong: that is where you learn to spot traps.
3. Space your repetitions

Flashcards with spaced repetition bring back the cards you miss sooner and the ones you know later. Ten minutes a day is enough to keep grape varieties, label terms, minimum ageing periods and service temperatures fresh until the exam.
4. Rehearse the real exam

In the last weeks, sit full mock exams with the real number of questions and the real time limit. Mock exams show you where you lose marks, train your pacing and remove the surprise factor on the day.
Keep a short list of your own recurring mistakes and reread it before every mock exam. Most errors repeat: the same two regions confused, the same label term misread.
How much study time do you really need?

Use the guideline hours as a minimum: about 6 hours for Level 1, around 26–28 hours for Level 2 and about 84 hours for Level 3, including class time. Spread them over the weeks before the exam rather than concentrating them.

A practical rule is to work backwards from your exam date. For Level 2, four to six weeks of 30–40 minutes a day covers the syllabus with time left for revision and mock exams. For Level 3, plan two to three months, with daily theory sessions, one written answer every day or two and regular tasting practice. If your exam is close, focus on the chapters with the most questions and on your weakest topics instead of trying to cover everything again.

Never practising under time pressure before the real exam.

The three WSET wine levels share the same goal, understanding what is in the glass, but they ask very different things of you. Level 1 checks that you know the main styles and grapes, Level 2 that you can connect grapes, regions and labels, and Level 3 that you can explain why a wine tastes the way it does.

Notice how the pass mark falls as the questions become harder. A 70% target at Level 1 sounds demanding, but the questions are simple; a 55% pass at Level 3 sounds generous, but you must reach it separately in the theory and in the tasting, and a strong result in one cannot compensate for the other.
WSET Wine Level 1: the first step
Level 1 is a short, beginner-friendly course on the main styles of wine, the principal grapes, storage and service, and food pairing. A few hours of focused practice are usually enough to feel ready.

The syllabus covers still, sparkling and fortified wines; how grape variety and climate shape style; the eight principal grapes (Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah); service temperatures and glasses; and how sweetness, acidity, salt and umami in food change the taste of a wine. With 90 seconds per question, time is rarely the issue: careless mistakes are, because 70% leaves room for only nine wrong answers.

Learn the food and wine interactions as a small table with arrows: sweet and umami food make wine taste more bitter and acidic; salt and acidity in food make it taste softer. Directions, not definitions, are what the questions test.
WSET Wine Level 2: grapes, regions and labels

Level 2 is the most popular wine qualification: it links the principal grapes and about 22 regionally important ones to more than 70 regions, and teaches how environment, winemaking and labels explain the wines you see on shelves.

The exam is 50 multiple-choice questions in one hour, with 55% to pass, 70% for merit and 85% for distinction. The questions reward connections: a region with its grape, a climate with its style, a label term with its meaning. Typical topics include oak and malolactic conversion, the traditional and tank methods for sparkling wine, Port and Sherry, and quality categories such as Crianza, Riserva, Kabinett or AOC/DOP.
How to prepare for Level 2
Build a grid for the eight principal grapes: climate, key regions, typical aromas, cool versus warm styles.
Learn regions as pairs with their grapes, then add the regionally important varieties country by country.
Turn labelling terms into flashcards and review them daily.
From three weeks before the exam, sit a full 50-question mock every week and aim for 70% to give yourself a margin.
WSET Wine Level 3: explain, write and taste
Level 3 asks you to explain causes and effects across the whole world of wine and to assess two wines blind. It is a significant step up and rewards regular study over two to three months.

The theory unit combines 50 multiple-choice questions with 4 short written answers, each split into parts where every mark rewards a correct, explained idea. The tasting unit asks for a full description of two wines with the systematic approach to tasting, including conclusions on quality and readiness for drinking; you are not asked to name the wine. You need at least 55% in each unit, and the units are marked separately.
How to prepare for Level 3
Study the vineyard and winemaking chapters thoroughly first: almost every regional question relies on them.
For each region, learn the chain climate → grape → winemaking → style → label.
Write one short answer every day or two and mark it against marking points: one idea per sentence, always with the "why".
Taste with the full systematic approach on every wine you drink, using only the exam vocabulary.
Sit timed theory mocks and practise two-wine blind flights in the final weeks.
Which wine level should you choose?

Start at Level 1 if wine is completely new, at Level 2 if you already know some grapes or work with wine, and at Level 3 after Level 2 or equivalent knowledge. Skipping Level 1 is common; skipping Level 2 is rarely a good idea.
You want a friendly introduction in a short time: Level 1.
You serve or sell wine, or simply want solid foundations: Level 2, with or without Level 1 first.
You hold Level 2 and want to understand the reasons behind styles and quality: Level 3.
You work in the trade and want the widely recognised professional standard: Level 3, and later the Diploma.

If you are unsure, try a few practice questions from each level. If Level 2 questions feel comfortable, you are probably ready to aim higher; if Level 1 questions already feel hard, start there and move on while the basics are fresh.
What comes after Level 3?

The next step is the Level 4 Diploma in Wines, a multi-unit professional qualification that requires Level 3 and takes many months of study. It is not part of this comparison, but it is worth knowing where the path leads.

The Diploma is organised in six units, D1 to D6, combining theory and tasting exams with a research assignment. Many people take Level 3 first simply to deepen their understanding and stop there; others use it as the foundation for a career in buying, education or wine writing. If the Diploma is your long-term goal, treat Level 3 as training in method: precise vocabulary, structured written answers and consistent tasting notes will all carry over. Common mistakes across the wine levels
The same few mistakes cost marks at every level. Most are about method rather than knowledge.
Confusing a grape with a place: Chablis is a region, Chardonnay is the grape.

Forgetting that the same grape tastes different in a cool and a warm climate.
Confusing sparkling methods: second fermentation in the bottle versus in a tank.
Leaving fortified wines, labelling terms and food pairing until the last week.
At Level 3, listing facts instead of explaining them, and using synonyms instead of the tasting terms the exam expects.
Whatever your level, review your mistakes before you add new material. A mistake you understand today is a question you will get right in the exam.

WSET mock exams: how to practise the real exam before the day

A WSET mock exam is a full practice paper sat with the real number of questions and the real time limit. Sitting two or three mocks in the final weeks, then reviewing every mistake, is the most effective way to find weak topics, train your pacing and walk into the exam without surprises.

You can know the syllabus well and still lose marks in the exam room: a question read too fast, a topic you never revised, a clock you forgot to watch. Mock exams exist to remove those risks before they count.
This page explains why mock exams work, how to sit one properly, how to review the result, what the format of each WSET level looks like, and how The Wine Goat simulates them for wine and spirits.
Why do mock exams matter for WSET?
Mock exams test what you can retrieve under time pressure, not what you recognise in your notes. They reveal your weak chapters, train your pacing and make the real exam feel familiar.

Practice questions by chapter are excellent while you learn, but they give you a hint: you know the topic before you read the question. In the real exam, a question on Sherry follows one on Riesling and another on storage. A mock exam mixes the whole syllabus exactly as the paper does, so it measures the knowledge you can actually use on the day.

Mock exams also give you a realistic score. If you consistently reach 70% or more in Level 2 mocks, you have a comfortable margin over the 55% pass mark. If you hover around the pass mark, you know you need to act on your weak topics before the exam, not after.

How to sit a mock exam in real conditions
Treat the mock like the real exam: one sitting, the real time limit, no notes, no phone and no pausing. The closer the conditions, the more useful the result.
Choose a quiet moment when you will not be interrupted for the whole duration.
Set the real time limit and do not stop the clock, even for one question.
Close your notes, textbook and other apps; the exam is closed book.
Answer every question, flagging the ones you are unsure about to revisit at the end.
Check the clock at the halfway point: at Level 2 you should be around question 25 after 30 minutes.
For Level 3 written answers, write in full sentences as you would on the day, not in notes.
Do your mock at the same time of day as your real exam if you can. Your concentration curve is part of what you are training.
How to review a mock exam
The review is where the progress happens: spend at least as long reviewing a mock as you spent sitting it. Classify every mistake, then fix the cause, not just the question.
Sort your mistakes into three types
Knowledge gaps: you did not know the fact. Go back to the lesson for that chapter and add the fact to your flashcards.
Confusions: you mixed up two similar things, such as two regions, two methods or two label terms. Build a small comparison of the pair.
Reading errors: you knew the answer but missed a word such as "not", "minimum" or "main". Slow down on the question stem.
Look at the chapter, not only the score

A total of 68% hides very different situations. Losing marks evenly across the syllabus means you need broad revision; losing half of them in one chapter means a targeted session will lift your score quickly. Check your results by topic and plan the next few days around the two or three weakest ones.
Read the explanations of correct answers too
Some correct answers were lucky guesses. If you hesitated, read the explanation anyway and learn why the other options are wrong: that is how you will recognise the same trap next time.
When should you sit mock exams?

Sit your first full mock about three weeks before the exam, then one per week, and a final light one two or three days before. Earlier than that, chapter questions are more useful because you have not covered the whole syllabus yet.

At Wine Level 3, a multiple-choice mock is only half of the rehearsal. Practise the written answers and the tasting under time pressure too, because they are where most marks are won or lost.

Each short written answer is divided into parts, and the marks for each part tell you how many separate ideas the examiner expects. Practise reading the question twice, underlining the command words (describe, explain, compare) and planning your points before writing. Common mistakes with mock exams
Mock exams only help if they are honest. These habits make them less useful.
Sitting the same mock again and again until you remember the answers rather than the reasons.
Pausing the clock or checking notes, which gives you a score you cannot trust.
Looking only at the final percentage and skipping the review.
Taking the first mock too late to act on the results.
At Level 3, skipping the written section because it takes longer to mark.
Panicking after one low score: a mock is a diagnosis, not a verdict.

Why do practice questions work?

Answering a question forces your memory to retrieve information, and every successful retrieval makes the next one easier. That is why testing yourself beats rereading, even when you get answers wrong.

Reading a chapter twice feels like progress because the text looks familiar. But familiarity is not recall: in the exam you have to produce the answer from memory, among three plausible alternatives. Practice questions train exactly that. They also show you, quickly and honestly, which topics you really know and which ones you only recognise.

Good questions come with explanations. A short note on why the right answer is right consolidates the fact; a deeper look at why each other option is wrong teaches you the distinctions the exam is built on, such as two regions that grow the same grape or two methods that sound alike.

Multiple-choice technique for WSET exams

Read the whole question, predict the answer before looking at the options, eliminate the clearly wrong ones and only then choose. Never leave a question blank: there is no penalty for a wrong answer at Levels 1 and 2.
Read the stem carefully

Many questions hinge on one word: "main", "typically", "minimum", "not", "most likely". Underline it mentally before you read the options. A question asking which grape is not permitted is the opposite of one asking which grape is typical, and in a hurry they look the same.
Predict, then compare
Try to answer before reading the four options. If your prediction is among them, it is very probably correct. If not, reread the question: you may have misread it.
Eliminate distractors

Wrong options are rarely absurd. They are often a real grape from the wrong region, a real technique with the wrong effect, or a correct fact that does not answer the question. Removing two options usually leaves a 50-50 choice you can reason through.
Manage your time
You have 90 seconds per question at Level 1 and 72 seconds at Level 2. Answer the easy ones quickly, flag the difficult ones and come back to them at the end with a fresh eye.
Change an answer only if you find a concrete reason, such as a word you misread. Second-guessing without new information more often turns a right answer into a wrong one.
Sample questions: Wine Level 1
Level 1 questions test the main grapes, styles, service and food pairing. They are short and direct; precision is what matters.
Which of these grape varieties is used to make white wine?
Merlot
Syrah
Riesling
Pinot Noir
Riesling is a white grape variety, one of the eight principal grapes. Merlot, Syrah and Pinot Noir are all black grapes used for red (and sometimes rosé) wines.
How does salt in food usually affect the taste of a wine?
It makes the wine taste less bitter and less acidic
It makes the wine taste more acidic
It makes the wine taste more bitter
It has no effect on the wine
Salt, like acidity in food, makes a wine taste softer: less bitter and less acidic. Sweetness and umami in food have the opposite effect, making wine taste more bitter and acidic.
Which of these wines should be served well chilled?
A sparkling wine
A full-bodied red
A medium-bodied red
An oaked red Rioja
Sparkling and sweet wines are served well chilled. Full- and medium-bodied reds are served at room temperature, while light-bodied reds can be lightly chilled.
Sample questions: Wine Level 2
Level 2 questions connect grapes, regions, winemaking and labels. Expect plausible distractors from the same country or technique family.
Sancerre, in the Loire Valley, is mainly made from which grape variety?
Chardonnay
Chenin Blanc
Sauvignon Blanc

Sancerre is a classic Loire Valley wine made from Sauvignon Blanc. Chenin Blanc is also a Loire grape, which makes it a typical distractor, but it is associated with other Loire appellations such as Vouvray.
What is the main effect of malolactic conversion on a wine?
It softens the acidity and can add buttery flavours
It increases the alcohol level
It adds tannin to the wine
It leaves residual sugar in the wine

Malolactic conversion turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, lowering the perceived acidity and often adding buttery notes. It does not change the alcohol level, add tannin or create sweetness.
Which method is typically used to make Prosecco?
The traditional method
The tank method
Carbonation
The transfer method

Prosecco is typically made by the tank method, with the second fermentation in a sealed tank, which preserves fresh, fruity aromas. The traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle, is used for Champagne.
Sample questions: Wine Level 3
Level 3 multiple-choice questions focus on causes and effects. Knowing the name is not enough: you must know why it matters.
What is the main effect of a large diurnal range on ripening grapes?
Cool nights help the grapes retain acidity and aromas
It increases the risk of hail
It reduces sugar accumulation during the day
It prevents tannins from ripening

A large difference between day and night temperatures lets grapes ripen in warm days while cool nights slow the loss of acidity and help preserve aromatic compounds. It is not linked to hail, and it does not stop sugar or tannin ripening.
What does extended lees contact typically add to a still white wine?
Tannin and colour
Body, texture and yeasty or bready notes
Higher acidity
Residual sweetness
Ageing on the lees adds body and a creamy texture, and can bring yeasty, bready flavours. Lees contact does not add tannin or colour, does not raise acidity and does not make a wine sweet.
How is the sweetness of Port achieved?
By adding sugar after fermentation
By drying the grapes before fermentation
By adding grape spirit during fermentation, which stops it
By blending in unfermented grape juice
Port is fortified during fermentation: the grape spirit raises the alcohol level and stops the yeast, leaving natural grape sugar in the wine. This is why Port is both sweet and high in alcohol.
Sample questions: Spirits
Spirits questions often test raw materials, legal rules and label terms. Numbers such as minimum percentages and ageing periods are easy marks once memorised.
What is a legal requirement for Bourbon?
It must be made in Kentucky
It must be made from 100% malted barley
It can use any grain, with no minimum
It must be made from a mash of at least 51% corn

Bourbon must be made from at least 51% corn and aged in new charred oak barrels. It can be made anywhere in the United States, not only in Kentucky; 100% malted barley is the rule for single malt whisky.
A Tequila labelled "joven" or "oro" is usually:
Aged for at least one year in oak
Unaged spirit, often with colour added
Made from a blend of Tequila and Mezcal
Aged in new charred oak barrels
Joven or oro (gold) Tequila is usually unaged, with colour added; the golden hue does not mean oak ageing. Reposado and añejo are the terms for Tequilas that have spent time in oak.
What is the minimum ageing for a Cognac labelled VSOP?
At least 10 years
At least 2 years
No minimum
At least 4 years
VSOP Cognac must be aged for at least four years in oak. VS requires at least two years and XO at least ten, so these terms make classic distractors for each other.
How to learn from a wrong answer
A wrong answer is the most useful thing a practice session can give you, provided you deal with it in three steps: understand it, connect it, and see it again later.
Understand: read the explanation and say in one sentence why the correct answer is right.
Connect: link the fact to something you already know, such as the climate of the region or the effect of the technique, so it is not an isolated detail.
Compare: if you confused two similar things, write the difference between them side by side.
Repeat: answer the same question again a few days later, and once more the week before the exam.

Flashcards work for WSET because they force you to recall a fact instead of rereading it, and spaced repetition brings back the cards you miss sooner than the ones you know. Most of a WSET exam is recall under time pressure: which grape makes Barolo, what Kabinett means on a German label, how long a VSOP Cognac must age. Flashcards are the most efficient way to make those facts stick, provided you build them well and review them on a schedule rather than when you happen to remember. This page explains why they work, what belongs on a good card, how to organise a deck for each level, and the short daily routine that turns a pile of cards into marks on exam day.
Why do flashcards work so well for WSET exams?

Flashcards work because every review is a small test: you see a prompt, you try to recall the answer, then you check. That effort of retrieval is what strengthens memory, far more than reading the same page of notes again.

Learning research calls this the testing effect, and it pairs naturally with a second principle, spacing. A fact reviewed once a day for a week is remembered for longer than the same fact crammed ten times in one evening. Spaced repetition simply organises this: each card has its own interval, which grows every time you answer correctly and shrinks when you get it wrong.

WSET exams reward exactly the kind of knowledge flashcards build. Multiple-choice questions often hinge on one precise detail, such as a minimum ageing period or the grape behind a regional name, and the wrong options are designed to look familiar. If you have only recognised a fact while reading, a plausible distractor can fool you. If you have retrieved it twenty times from a blank prompt, it will not.
How spaced repetition decides what you see
In a spaced-repetition system, each answer moves the card along a ladder of intervals. A typical progression looks like this:

The result is that your daily review time goes where it is needed: on the handful of facts you keep confusing, not on the ones you have known for weeks.
What should you put on a WSET flashcard?

Put one fact, or one cause-and-effect link, on each card, written as a question you can answer in a few seconds. Small cards are reviewed faster, failed more honestly and scheduled more precisely than big ones.
The syllabus for every level breaks down into a few families of facts. These are the ones that deserve cards:
Grape varieties: colour, typical aromas, and how the style changes from a cool to a warm climate (Chardonnay in Chablis versus Chardonnay in a warm Californian site).
Region and grape pairs: Sancerre and Sauvignon Blanc, Rioja and Tempranillo, Barossa Valley and Shiraz, Chianti and Sangiovese.
Label terms: Riserva, Crianza, Reserva, Kabinett, Spätlese, Brut, Extra Brut, Premier Cru, AOC/DOP, VS, VSOP, XO, reposado, añejo.
Key numbers: minimum ageing periods, minimum percentages of a raw material, exam-relevant temperatures for serving.
Processes and their effects: malolactic conversion, lees contact, carbonic maceration, pot versus column still, traditional versus tank method.
Food and wine interactions: what sweetness, umami, salt and acidity in food do to a wine.
For Level 3: causes and effects you will need in written answers, such as why a high diurnal range keeps acidity in the grapes.
Five rules for a good card
One answer per card. 'Name the three main grapes of Champagne' becomes three easier cards, or one card that asks for all three only once each grape is secure.
Ask in both directions for pairs. 'Barolo: which grape?' and 'Nebbiolo: name two famous wines' are two different memories.
Prefer 'why' to 'what' as you advance. 'Why is Mosel Riesling often light in alcohol?' trains the reasoning the exam wants.
Use the exam's vocabulary. Write 'pronounced', 'medium(+)', 'high acidity', not your own synonyms.
Add a short hook on the back: a map position, a contrast or a memorable example, so the answer has something to attach to.

A 15-minute daily flashcard routine
Review the cards that are due every day, before adding new ones. Ten to fifteen minutes is enough for most learners, and consistency matters far more than session length.
Minutes 1–8: clear the cards due today. Answer out loud or in your head before turning the card, and be strict: a half-remembered answer counts as wrong.
Minutes 8–12: add five to ten new cards from the chapter you are studying.
Minutes 12–15: look at the cards you failed and ask why. Are two grapes or two regions blurring together? Make a contrast card that puts them side by side.
Once a week: take a set of practice questions on the same chapters to check that the flashcard knowledge transfers to exam-style questions.

Common flashcard mistakes
Most flashcard problems come from cards that are too big, reviews that are too generous, or a deck that grows faster than you can review it.
Cards that hold a whole region. 'Bordeaux' as a front with ten lines on the back cannot be answered honestly. Split it into Left Bank grapes, Right Bank grapes, climate, key appellations.
Marking yourself right when you were close. The schedule only works if you are honest; a near miss should come back soon.
Only one direction. Knowing that Rioja is Tempranillo does not guarantee you can name a Spanish region for Tempranillo.
Skipping days, then bingeing. Missed reviews pile up; a short daily session keeps the queue small.
Using flashcards alone. Cards build facts; practice questions and mock exams test whether you can use them under exam conditions.

Do flashcards really help for WSET exams?

Yes. WSET multiple-choice questions often turn on a single precise fact, such as a grape, a label term or an ageing minimum, and the wrong options are designed to look familiar. Flashcards train active recall of exactly those facts, and spaced repetition keeps them fresh until exam day. Combine them with practice questions so you also learn to handle distractors.
How many flashcards should I review each day?

Review all the cards that are due, then add five to ten new ones. For most learners this takes 10 to 15 minutes. If your due pile keeps growing beyond 20 minutes, stop adding new cards for a few days and let the queue settle. Daily consistency matters more than the number of cards.
What is spaced repetition?

Spaced repetition is a review schedule in which each card has its own interval. When you answer correctly the interval grows, so you see the card less often; when you miss it the interval shrinks and the card comes back soon. Your study time goes to the facts you are about to forget, not to the ones you already know well.
Should I make my own flashcards or use ready-made ones?

Both have value. Ready-made cards save time and follow the syllabus structure, so nothing important is left out. Writing a few of your own cards for the facts you personally keep confusing adds a second layer of memory. A good approach is to start from a ready-made deck and add contrast cards for your weak spots.
Are flashcards useful for WSET Level 3 written answers?

Yes, if you write cause-and-effect cards rather than single names. Cards such as 'Why does a high diurnal range help acidity?' rehearse the explanations the written questions reward. Flashcards will not replace practising full written answers, but they make the building blocks of those answers fast and reliable.
When should I start using flashcards before the exam?

From the first week of study. Spaced repetition needs time to work: a card first learned two days before the exam has had no chance to move into long-term memory. Start making cards as soon as you begin each chapter, so that by the final weeks you are reviewing, not learning facts for the first time.

How do you build a WSET study plan from your exam date?

Count the weeks between today and the exam, subtract one week as a buffer, and divide the rest into three phases: learning (about half), consolidation (about a third) and final revision (the remainder). Then turn each week into a short daily goal.

Working backwards protects you from the most common planning failure: spending too long on the first chapters and rushing the last ones. It also makes the workload visible. If you have 84 hours of study to fit into six weeks, you will see straight away that you need about two hours a day, and you can decide whether to start earlier or accept a lighter target.

Choosing the right WSET level
How many WSET wine and spirits levels are there?

Wine has four levels: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 and the Level 4 Diploma. Spirits has three: Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3. Each level adds depth and a new kind of assessment. Levels 1 and 2 are tested with multiple-choice questions only, while Level 3 adds short written answers and a blind tasting, and the Diploma is a multi-unit programme for professionals.
Do I have to take Level 1 before Level 2?

No. Level 2, in both wine and spirits, is designed for people with little or no prior knowledge, so many learners start there. Level 1 is still a good choice if you want a gentle introduction or a quick certificate for a new job in hospitality. Level 3 is a different matter: Level 2 or equivalent knowledge is recommended before you enrol.
Which WSET level do I need to work in wine?

Level 2 is a solid foundation for restaurant service, retail and wholesale, because it covers the grapes, regions and label terms you meet every day. Level 3 is widely seen as the professional standard for buyers, sommeliers, educators and sales roles, since it trains you to explain why wines taste as they do. The Diploma is for those aiming at senior or expert positions.
Should I study wine or spirits first?

Start with the drinks you work with or enjoy most, because motivation and real-life examples make studying much easier. The two pathways are independent: you do not need a wine qualification to take a spirits course, or the reverse. Some topics overlap, such as tasting technique, oak and service, so the second pathway usually feels lighter once you have completed a level of the first.
Exam format and study time
What is the format of the WSET Level 1 exam?

Both Wine Level 1 and Spirits Level 1 are tested with 30 multiple-choice questions in 45 minutes. You need 70%, which means 21 correct answers, to pass, and there are no higher grades. Each question has four options and one correct answer. The pass mark is high because the questions are straightforward, so careless mistakes matter more than difficult ones.
What is the format of the WSET Level 2 exam?

Wine Level 2 and Spirits Level 2 each have 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. A pass needs 55% (28 correct answers), a merit 70% and a distinction 85%. Questions often test precise details such as label terms, minimum ageing periods or the grape behind a regional name, so a broad overview gives a pass while the higher grades need detail.
What is the format of the WSET Level 3 wine exam?

Wine Level 3 has two units. The theory paper combines 50 multiple-choice questions with 4 short written answers, and the tasting unit asks you to assess two wines blind using the Systematic Approach to Tasting. You need at least 55% in each unit, and a strong theory score cannot make up for a weak tasting. Higher results earn a merit or a distinction.
How long does it take to prepare for each level?

WSET's guideline study time, including class hours, is about 6 hours for Level 1, about 28 hours for Wine Level 2 (about 26 for Spirits Level 2) and about 84 hours for Level 3. In practice, most learners prepare Level 1 in one or two weeks, Level 2 in four to six weeks and Level 3 in ten to sixteen weeks of regular daily study.
Do wrong answers cost marks in the multiple-choice papers?

No. Each correct answer earns one mark and a wrong answer simply earns nothing, so you should never leave a question blank. If you are unsure, eliminate the options you know are wrong and choose among the rest. Practising with timed questions helps you manage this calmly: at Level 2 you have about 72 seconds per question, which is usually enough.
Preparing effectively
What is the best way to prepare for a WSET exam?

Use active methods rather than rereading. Learn each chapter, then test yourself straight away with practice questions; build key facts into flashcards reviewed with spaced repetition; review every mistake; and take timed mock exams in the final weeks. Short daily sessions work better than long weekend ones. For Level 3, practise written answers and tasting notes from the very start.
How can I practise blind tasting for Level 3?

Taste regularly and write a full note on every wine using the Systematic Approach to Tasting: appearance, nose, palate and conclusions on quality. Use the exam's exact terms, because synonyms do not score. Ask someone to pour wines for you without showing the bottle, compare classic styles side by side, and justify quality with balance, length, intensity and complexity.
Are practice questions online the same as the real exam questions?

No. Real exam papers are confidential, and no app or website can offer them. Good practice questions, like those in The Wine Goat, are written to reflect the published syllabus and the exam format, so they train the same knowledge and the same skill of choosing between plausible options. Treat them as training, not as a preview of your paper.
How many mock exams should I take?

Two to four full mocks is a good target for Level 2, and at least three for Level 3, spread over the final third of your preparation. Take the first one early enough to act on the result. Run each mock under real conditions, with the timer on and no notes, then spend more time reviewing your mistakes than you spent on the mock itself.

Can you prepare for a wine and a spirits level at the same time?

Make the daily goal small enough to meet on a bad day, track your streak and chapter progress, and connect study to real bottles you open or serve. Seeing a weak chapter move from 50% to 80% in practice questions is far more motivating than counting hours. If motivation drops, shorten sessions rather than skipping them: ten minutes of flashcards keeps the habit and the memory alive.
What should I do the morning of a WSET exam?

Keep it light. Eat normally, review a short set of flashcards or your list of personal confusions for ten to fifteen minutes, then stop. Check the time, place or online set-up and what your course provider asks you to bring. Arrive or log in early so you start calm. A glossary of wine terms you meet at every level
These terms appear across the wine levels, with growing precision. Learn a one-line definition early and add detail as you move up.
One-line definition
Body
The overall sense of weight and richness of a wine in the mouth, mostly from alcohol and sugar
Tannin
A compound from grape skins, seeds and oak that gives red wines a drying, grippy feel
Acidity
The fresh, mouth-watering element of a wine; cool climates generally keep more of it
Malolactic conversion
A process that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, sometimes with buttery notes
Lees
Dead yeast cells left after fermentation; contact with them adds texture and bready or biscuit notes
Traditional method
Sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in the bottle, as in Champagne
Tank method
Sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in a sealed tank, as for most Prosecco
Fortification
Adding grape spirit to wine, during or after fermentation, as for Port and Sherry
Noble rot
A fungus that concentrates sugar in grapes and is behind some famous sweet wines

The difference between day and night temperatures; cool nights help keep acidity

A legally defined place name with rules on grapes, yields and winemaking

Shorthand for the traditional European regions and the regions outside Europe
Moving up a level: what changes in the way you study
Each step up asks for a new study skill, not just more facts. Changing the way you study at the start of the new level saves weeks of frustration.
From Level 1 to Level 2

At Level 1, a list of eight grapes and a few rules is enough. At Level 2 the volume of names multiplies, and the challenge becomes organisation. Stop learning grapes and regions as separate lists and start building pairs and grids: a region always comes with its grape, its climate and its typical style. Flashcards become essential at this point, because recognition alone will not separate two regions in the same country.
From Level 2 to Level 3

Level 3 adds two new skills: writing explanations and tasting accurately. Many strong Level 2 candidates are surprised by their first written answers, which tend to be lists of correct words without the reasons that earn the marks. Start writing short answers in the first weeks, not after you finish the regions. Do the same with tasting: one structured note per wine you drink, with the exam vocabulary, is worth more than an occasional long tasting session.
Before you start the next level
Keep your flashcards from the previous level and review them weekly: Level 3 assumes everything from Level 2.
Revisit the vineyard and winemaking basics before you meet the new regions.
Taste a few classic wines you studied, so names become real flavours.
Set the exam date early, so your plan has a clear end point.
Choosing a level: three typical situations
Real decisions depend on background, goals and time. These short examples show how candidates usually decide.
A new restaurant server who wants to talk confidently about the wine list in a month: Level 2, with Level 1 skipped, because the regions and label terms on a wine list are Level 2 content.
An enthusiast who has enjoyed wine for years but never studied it, with only two free weekends: Level 1 now, then Level 2 when there is time for several weeks of regular study.
A shop assistant who passed Level 2 with merit and is starting to advise customers on fine wine: Level 3, planned over about three months, with tasting built into every week.
A career changer aiming at buying or education roles: Level 2 and Level 3 in sequence, keeping in mind that the Diploma usually follows for those paths.
If you cannot decide between two levels, look at the practice questions for the higher one. If you can answer around half of them before studying, that level is a realistic target.
Can I take WSET Wine Level 3 without Level 2?

Level 3 recommends Level 2 or equivalent knowledge, and some course providers may accept proven experience instead. In practice, skipping Level 2 is rarely wise: Level 3 assumes you already know the principal grapes, regions and label terms, and spends its time on explaining why. If you want to test yourself, try Level 2 practice questions first; frequent gaps there are a sign to build those foundations before Level 3.
Is there a tasting exam at WSET Wine Level 2?

No. Wine Level 2 is assessed only by 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. Tasting is still part of the course and helps you remember styles, because a grape you have tasted is easier to recall than one you have only read about. Writing short notes with the systematic approach at Level 2 is also good training if you plan to continue to Level 3, where tasting has its own unit.
How much time should I leave between Level 2 and Level 3?

There is no fixed rule. Some candidates move on within a few weeks while Level 2 knowledge is fresh, others take a few months to gain tasting experience. What matters is that Level 2 content is still secure when you start: review your Level 2 flashcards and practice questions before the course, and plan two to three months of regular study for Level 3 itself.
Which grapes do I need to know for WSET Wine Level 2?

The eight principal grapes are central: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah. Around these, Level 2 adds about 22 regionally important varieties linked to their key regions, such as Tempranillo in Rioja, Sangiovese in Chianti or Nebbiolo in Barolo. Learn each one with its regions, climate and typical style rather than as an isolated name.
Is WSET Wine Level 2 enough to work in a wine shop or restaurant?

For many roles in retail, service and wholesale, Level 2 gives a solid working foundation: you will understand the grapes, regions and label terms you meet every day. Employers' expectations vary, and roles involving buying, fine wine or training often look for Level 3. Whatever the role, combining the qualification with regular tasting of the wines you actually sell makes the knowledge useful straight away.

How do I simulate WSET exam conditions at home?

Choose a quiet place and a time you will not be interrupted, set the real time limit, and put away notes, books and your phone. Answer every question without pausing the clock. If your real exam is on a computer, practise on a screen; if it is on paper, try noting your answers by hand. Small details like these make the real day feel familiar.
What if my mock exam scores are getting worse?

First, check whether the mocks are comparable: a new mock may cover chapters you studied long ago, which is exactly what it should reveal. Look at the scores by chapter rather than the total. A drop usually comes from older topics fading, which means your flashcard and mixed-question reviews need more time. Fix those chapters, then sit another mock a few days later.
How long should I spend reviewing a mock exam?

At least as long as the mock itself: about an hour for a Level 2 mock, and more for Level 3 written answers. Go through every wrong answer and every lucky guess, classify the mistake, read the explanation and decide one concrete action for each topic. A rushed five-minute review wastes most of the value of the mock.
Should I take a mock exam the day before the real exam?

Usually not. A full mock the day before can tire you and shake your confidence if one score is lower than expected. Sit your last full mock two or three days before the exam, then use the final day for light flashcards and your list of personal confusions. Rest is part of the preparation.
Are mock exams useful for WSET Level 1?

Yes, even though the exam is short. Level 1 needs 70% to pass, so careless mistakes matter more than at higher levels. Two timed mocks of 30 questions in 45 minutes in the final days show whether any chapter is weak and train you to read every question carefully. Review each mistake straight away; at this level, most are quick to fix.
Anatomy of a WSET-style question

Every multiple-choice question has three parts: a stem that asks the question, one key that answers it, and three distractors built from real facts used in the wrong place. Seeing the structure helps you read questions the way they were written.

Take a typical Level 2 item: "Which grape variety is mainly used for red Rioja?" The key is Tempranillo. The distractors might be Garnacha, which is genuinely grown in Rioja but is not the main grape; Nebbiolo, a famous black grape from the wrong country; and Malbec, a grape strongly associated with another region. Each wrong option tests a different confusion: a real partner grape, a real grape from another place, and a well-known name that sounds plausible. The word "mainly" is what turns Garnacha from tempting into wrong.

Eight more sample questions
These questions mix levels and include more demanding distractors. Answer each one before opening the explanation, and notice which kind of distractor tempted you.
Chianti Classico is mainly made from which grape variety?
Nebbiolo
Sangiovese
Montepulciano
Barbera

Chianti, in Tuscany, is based on Sangiovese. Nebbiolo and Barbera are Piedmont grapes, and Montepulciano is a grape grown mainly in central and southern Italy, which makes it a classic "sounds like the region" trap.
What does the term "Brut" indicate on a sparkling wine label?
A sweet style
A wine made by the tank method
A dry style
A wine aged at least five years
Brut is a sweetness term and indicates a dry style. It says nothing about the production method or the ageing period, which are what the other options describe.
Why are vineyards in cool regions of the Northern Hemisphere often planted on south-facing slopes?
To catch more sunlight and warmth
To protect the vines from rain
To increase yields
To reduce sugar in the grapes
South-facing slopes receive more direct sunlight in the Northern Hemisphere, helping grapes ripen in marginal climates. Better ripening increases sugar rather than reducing it.
Which winemaking technique is most associated with the fruity red wines of Beaujolais?
Extended oak ageing
Lees stirring
Carbonic maceration

Whole bunches fermenting in a carbon dioxide-rich environment give the soft tannins and bright red-fruit, sometimes banana-like, aromas typical of many Beaujolais wines. Lees stirring is mainly a white winemaking technique.
Which type of still typically produces a lighter, more neutral spirit?
A pot still
A column still
Both produce the same style
Neither; style depends only on the raw material
A column still allows continuous distillation to high strength, removing more flavour compounds and giving a lighter, more neutral spirit. Pot stills generally give fuller, more flavourful spirits.
What is Tequila made from?
Sugar cane
Barley
Blue agave
Grapes
Tequila is made from blue agave. Sugar cane is the raw material of rum, barley of many whiskies and grapes of brandy, each a real raw material for the wrong spirit.
What is the minimum ageing for Scotch whisky?
Three years in oak in Scotland
Two years in any cask
One year in new oak
There is no minimum
Scotch whisky must be matured in oak casks in Scotland for at least three years. The other options borrow numbers and rules that belong to other categories.
What is the main difference between a Fino and an Oloroso Sherry?
Fino is sweet, Oloroso is dry
Fino ages under a layer of flor, Oloroso ages oxidatively
Fino is made from black grapes
Oloroso is not fortified

Fino matures under flor, a layer of yeast that protects it from oxygen and keeps it pale and fresh; Oloroso matures without flor, developing a darker colour and nutty flavours. Both are fortified and both are made dry.

Mini case: stuck at 60%

A Level 2 candidate has scored around 60% in mixed sets for two weeks. More questions alone have not helped. The fix starts with the data: sorting the last 100 wrong answers shows that a third are confusions between regions in the same country and a quarter are misread stems. The candidate builds ten contrast cards for the confused pairs, reads every stem twice for qualifiers, and practises in smaller, slower sets for a week. Mixed scores climb towards 70%, because the problem was never a lack of effort but a few repeated patterns.
Are WSET multiple-choice questions designed to be tricky?

They are designed to be precise rather than tricky. Wrong options are usually real facts placed in the wrong context, so a vague memory is not enough. Read the full stem, look for qualifiers such as "main" or "minimum", predict the answer before reading the options and eliminate what does not fit. Candidates who learn grapes, regions and processes as linked pairs find most questions straightforward.
Should I start practice questions before I finish the course?

Yes. Start with questions on each chapter as soon as you have studied it, even in the first week. Early testing shows what did not stick while the lesson is still fresh, and it strengthens memory more than rereading. Leave full mixed mock exams for later, when you have covered most of the syllabus, but do not wait until the end to start testing yourself.
What practice score shows I am ready for the exam?

Look for consistent scores in mixed sets and mocks comfortably above the threshold you are aiming for. At Level 2, many candidates use about 70% in mixed practice as a sign of a safe pass, and around 85% or more for a realistic distinction attempt. Check chapter scores too: one very weak chapter can cost several marks on the day.
Can I practise WSET questions in my own language?

In The Wine Goat you can practise in English, Italian, French or Spanish, with separate versions for Spain and Argentina. A useful approach is to learn difficult concepts in the language you think in and then answer questions in the language of your exam, so the exact terminology becomes familiar before the day.

Worked example: turning one lesson into ten cards
After a lesson on the Loire Valley for Level 2, a good deck takes about five minutes to build and covers each idea once. Here is how one lesson becomes ten focused cards.

Pouilly-Fumé: which grape? → Sauvignon Blanc.

Flashcards for tasting vocabulary at Level 3
The tasting unit rewards precise, consistent vocabulary, and flashcards are an efficient way to learn it. Build cards for the scales themselves and for the typical structure of classic wines.
Scales: which levels exist for acidity, tannin, body, flavour intensity and finish, and in what order.
Typical structures: the expected acidity of a cool-climate white, the tannin level of a classic Nebbiolo, the body of a fortified wine.
Quality reasoning: the four indicators used to justify a quality assessment, balance, length, intensity and complexity.
Readiness for drinking: what makes a wine suitable for further ageing or best drunk now.
Aroma clusters: grouping descriptors into families such as citrus, stone fruit, red fruit or spice.

Then use the cards at the table: after reviewing the acidity scale, describe the acidity of the wine you are drinking and check it against what you expected. Vocabulary that is used straight away is remembered for much longer.
When the review queue gets out of hand

If you miss a week and find several hundred cards due, do not try to clear them all at once. Stop adding new cards, review a fixed number each day (for example 100, or 15–20 minutes) starting with the cards closest to the exam topics, and let the queue shrink over a few days. Once it is back under control, restart new cards at a slower rate. Most people who abandon flashcards do so at this point; a calm, fixed daily quota is what keeps the habit alive.
Are paper flashcards or digital flashcards better for WSET?

Both work if you use them every day. Paper cards are good for making cards, which itself helps memory, but scheduling them by hand is hard once the deck grows. Digital flashcards with spaced repetition handle the scheduling for you, show each card exactly when it is due and fit into short moments on a phone. Many candidates use ready-made digital cards and add a few of their own.
How do I remember numbers like minimum ageing periods?

Put each number on its own card, ask for it in both directions and attach it to a pattern. For Cognac, for example, learn VS, VSOP and XO as a sequence rather than three separate facts. Review number cards daily in the last two weeks, because these are easy marks in multiple-choice questions and the distractors usually use real numbers from other categories.
Can I use flashcards for WSET spirits exams?

Yes, and they suit spirits particularly well. Spirits Level 1 and Level 2 include many precise facts: raw materials, still types, legal requirements, minimum ageing and label terms such as VS, VSOP, XO, reposado or añejo. Build cards by category and add contrast cards for similar spirits, then check with practice questions that the facts hold up when the options look alike.
Should my flashcards be in the same language as my exam?

Ideally, the terms on your cards should match the language of your exam, because label terms and tasting vocabulary must be recognised instantly. You can still write explanations on the back in the language you think in. In The Wine Goat you can switch language, which helps if you learn in one language and sit the exam in another.

Planning around an intensive or weekend course

If your course is condensed into a few days, split your private study into three blocks: a light start before the course, consolidation straight after it, and a rehearsal phase before the exam. The days of the course itself are for listening, tasting and taking notes, not for extra study.

Planning a second attempt

If you need to resit an exam or a unit, do not restart the whole plan from the beginning. Start with a full mock to see what is still secure, then build a shorter plan around the chapters, or the unit, that cost you marks.

A second attempt usually needs four to six weeks for a multiple-choice paper: one week of diagnosis and targeted lessons, two or three weeks of mixed questions with heavy work on the weak chapters, and a final phase of timed mocks. For a Level 3 unit, focus the plan on that unit only: daily written answers marked against marking points for the theory, or two to three full tasting notes a week for the tasting. Keep your old flashcards running throughout, so the topics you already knew stay safe.
A weekly review ritual
Once a week, take ten minutes to check the plan against reality. Small adjustments every week prevent the large, discouraging rewrites that make people give up.
Compare what you planned with what you did, without judgement.
Check your scores by chapter: which two chapters are weakest?
Move one session next week onto each of those chapters.
Check the flashcard queue: if it keeps growing, add fewer new cards next week.
Confirm the next mock date and protect it in your calendar.
Keep your weekly review on the same day each week, for example Sunday evening. The habit matters more than the exact day.
How many hours a week should I study for WSET Level 3?

Spread over about twelve weeks, Level 3 usually means five to seven hours of private study a week, on top of any class time. In practice that is 45–60 minutes most days, with a slightly longer slot for timed written answers or tasting. Weeks spent on large regions and winemaking can be heavier, and the final weeks shift towards mocks and reviewing mistakes.
Can I prepare for two WSET levels at the same time?

It is possible but rarely efficient. If you must, for example Wine Level 2 and Spirits Level 1 within a few weeks, give each exam its own daily slot and its own flashcard deck, and prioritise the earlier exam until it is done. Avoid preparing two levels of the same subject at once: the higher level assumes the lower one is already secure.
How do I plan if I do not have an exam date yet?

Pick a provisional date that matches the comfortable window for your level and plan backwards from it, as if it were fixed. A date, even a provisional one, turns open-ended study into a plan with phases and a daily goal. Once you book the real exam, adjust the phases. Without a date, it is easy to stay in the learning phase indefinitely.
How do I keep a study plan with shift work?

Plan by sessions rather than by days of the week. Decide how many sessions you need each week, then place them when your rota is published, preferring times when you are rested. Keep flashcards for short breaks and commutes, and put mock exams on days off. A minimum daily goal of ten minutes on working days keeps the memory and the habit going.
Should I plan rest days in my WSET study plan?

Yes. One light or free day a week makes a plan easier to keep and gives you a natural buffer when life gets in the way. On a rest day, a few minutes of flashcards is enough to keep reviews from piling up. Avoid long breaks of several days in the final month, when regular contact with the material matters most.

How the mistakes review and spaced repetition work together

The app keeps two memories of your weak points: the questions you got wrong and the flashcards you missed. Both are brought back on a schedule, so your time is spent on what you have not yet mastered rather than on what you already know.

When you miss a question, it is saved to your personal review with its explanation and the reasons why the other options are wrong. When you return to it a few days later and answer correctly, it moves further away; if you miss it again, it comes back sooner. Flashcards follow the same logic with their own intervals. Over a few weeks, the review becomes a precise map of your remaining gaps, and that map is exactly what you need in the final phase before the exam.
Using the Wine Level 3 tools

Open questions with model answers

Each of the 101 open questions asks you to explain, describe or compare, as a short written answer does. Write your answer first, then compare it with the model answer and the marking points. Maps make regions easier to place and connect with their climate: a river, a coast or a mountain range often explains the style of the wine. Films and podcasts help you picture vineyard and cellar techniques and are useful when you cannot sit down with a lesson, for example while travelling.

Can I use The Wine Goat without an exam date?

Yes. You can study the lessons, questions, flashcards and games for any available level at your own pace, which suits enthusiasts who want to learn wine or spirits properly without sitting an exam yet. The personal study plan works best with a date, though, because it spreads the chapters across the weeks and sets the daily goal. A provisional date is a good compromise.
How much time do I need to spend in the app each day?

It depends on your level and target grade. As a guide, about 15–20 minutes for Level 1, around 30 minutes for Level 2 and 45–60 minutes for Level 3, split into short sessions if that suits you. The app sets a daily goal from your exam date and target grade; meeting it consistently matters more than occasional long sessions.
Does The Wine Goat replace my WSET course?

No. You still enrol with a WSET course provider, who teaches the course, runs guided tastings and organises the exam. The Wine Goat is an independent study app that helps you remember and practise what the course teaches, with lessons, practice questions, flashcards, mock exams and a study plan between and after your classes.
What are the games in the app for?

The games, survival, match-it and lightning quiz, train fast recall in a lighter format. They are ideal for short breaks or tired evenings when a full lesson feels like too much, and they keep your streak going. They complement the core work of lessons, questions, flashcards and mock exams rather than replacing it.
Can I practise the Level 3 tasting in the app without opening wine?

Partly. The blind-tasting trainer teaches the structure of the systematic approach, the scales and the vocabulary, and you can learn those away from the glass with flashcards and lessons. The tasting unit, though, tests what you perceive in real wines, so the trainer is most useful when you have a glass in front of you. Aim to combine both: vocabulary on the go, full notes whenever you taste.
Does The Wine Goat work for spirits as well as wine?

Tasting and practical skills
Do I need to taste a lot of wine to pass Level 2?

No. Wine Level 2 is assessed only by multiple-choice questions, so you can pass without tasting widely. Tasting still helps memory: a grape or region you have tasted becomes a real flavour rather than a name on a list. A few classic examples of the principal grapes, tasted side by side with a short structured note, are often enough to make the theory stick. Sharing bottles with other candidates keeps it affordable and adds discussion.
How many wines should I taste before the Level 3 tasting exam?

There is no magic number, but regular practice matters more than volume. Aim to write a full note with the systematic approach for two or three wines a week from the start of your preparation, and more in the final month. Include the classic styles of the syllabus and taste some wines blind, poured by someone else, so you learn to describe what is in the glass instead of what the label tells you.
Do I have to identify the wine in the Level 3 tasting?

No. You describe each wine with the systematic approach and reach conclusions on quality and readiness for drinking, but you are not asked to name the grape, region or vintage. Marks come from accurate descriptions of appearance, nose and palate and from a quality assessment justified with balance, length, intensity and complexity. Guessing the wine earns nothing, so focus on precise, consistent observations.
Spirits preparation
What does the WSET Spirits Level 2 exam cover?

Spirits Level 2 has 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. Fourteen questions cover production, 23 the principal spirits such as whiskies, brandies, rum, Tequila and vodka, 7 flavoured spirits and aromatised wines, and 6 service and cocktails. Because almost half the paper is on the principal spirits, their legal rules, ageing requirements and label terms deserve the largest share of your study time.
Is spirits harder than wine at the same level?

Neither is harder overall; they are different. Spirits involves more production detail, such as stills and maturation, and many legal rules and ageing minimums. Wine involves more geography, with dozens of regions linked to grapes. Candidates with a bar background often find spirits easier to picture, while those who work in restaurants or shops may feel at home with wine. Choose the one that fits your work and interest.
Can I prepare for Spirits Level 3 in the app?

Not yet. Spirits Level 3, like the Wine Diploma, is in preparation in The Wine Goat. Today the app covers Spirits Level 1, which is free with about 210 questions, and Spirits Level 2, with about 1,000 questions, alongside lessons, flashcards, mock exams and a study plan. Spirits Level 3 adds written answers and a blind tasting of two spirits, so a solid Level 2 foundation is the best preparation in the meantime.
Exam day and after
What happens if I fail a WSET exam?

You can usually resit the exam, or at Level 3 only the unit you did not pass, through your course provider, which sets the dates and conditions. Use your result as a diagnosis: sit a full mock to see what is still secure, then build a shorter plan around the chapters or the unit that cost you marks. Most candidates who resit with a targeted plan improve clearly on the second attempt.
Can I take a WSET exam online?

Some course providers offer certain exams online with remote supervision, while others hold all exams in person. Ask your provider which formats are available for your level and what the technical requirements are. If you sit online, rehearse your mocks on the same device and in the same room, so the set-up feels familiar and nothing distracts you on the day.
How should I use my time in the exam room?

Work through the paper once at a steady pace, answering the questions you are sure about and flagging doubtful ones. Check the clock at the halfway point, then return to your flagged questions with the time left. Change an answer only if you find a concrete reason. At Level 3, keep enough time for the written answers and write in full sentences, one explained idea per sentence.
Studying in practice
Is self-study with an app enough without a study group?

Many candidates prepare alone successfully, because practice questions, flashcards and mock exams give the feedback a group would. A study partner adds something different: shared tastings, explaining topics to each other and keeping motivation up. If you study alone, use the explanations in each question as your second opinion and consider at least a few tasting sessions with other people, especially at Level 3.
Can I prepare on my phone only?

Yes, most daily preparation works well on a phone: lessons, questions, flashcards and games are designed for short sessions. For mock exams and Level 3 written answers, a larger screen or a quiet desk helps you concentrate and type comfortably. A good mix is phone for the daily goal and a computer or tablet for timed mocks.
